A pie is a baked dish made of a filling (the food inside) that is enclosed in, covered by, or sitting inside a layer of pastry, which is called the crust. The crust is a simple dough made from flour, fat (usually butter or lard), and a little water. When baked, it turns firm, golden, and often flaky — functioning as an edible container that holds the filling together.

The simplest way to picture a pie: a shell of baked dough with food inside it.

Pie fillings fall into two broad categories:

Sweet pies are desserts. The filling is made from fruit, sugar, custard, cream, or nuts. Common examples include apple pie, cherry pie, blueberry pie, pumpkin pie, pecan pie, banana cream pie, and chocolate cream pie. These are served at the end of a meal or as a treat.

Savory pies are main-course or snack foods. The filling is made from meat, vegetables, gravy, or cheese. Common examples include chicken pot pie (chunks of chicken and vegetables in a creamy sauce), steak and kidney pie (a British classic), pork pie (cold-cut meat in a firm pastry shell), and quiche (a pie-like dish filled with eggs, cream, and often cheese or vegetables).

Not all pies are built the same way. The crust can be arranged in several patterns:

  • Double-crust (full crust): Pastry on both the bottom and the top, fully enclosing the filling. Classic apple pie is a well-known example.
  • Single-crust (open-face): Pastry only on the bottom, with the filling left exposed on top. Pumpkin pie is a good example.
  • Top-crust only: The filling sits directly in the dish, and a pastry lid is placed only on top. Chicken pot pie is often made this way.
  • Shell only (pre-baked shell): The crust is baked empty first (called "blind baking"), then filled with an unbaked filling — like whipped cream, ice cream, or chilled custard. Banana cream pie is made this way.

A few foods are called "pies" but bend the usual rules slightly:

  • Shepherd's pie / Cottage pie: These are called pies, but instead of a pastry crust, the topping is a layer of mashed potato. The concept is the same — a savory filling covered by a topping — but technically there is no pastry. Shepherd's pie uses lamb; cottage pie uses beef.
  • Pizza pie: In American English (especially older usage), a pizza is sometimes called a "pizza pie" because of its round shape and layered structure.
  • Cream pie / Ice cream pie: These are fully valid pies, but the filling is not baked — it's added to the pre-baked shell after cooling.

"Pie" is used in several important expressions. These are not literal pies — they use the idea of a pie (something whole that can be divided and shared) to talk about abstract ideas.

"A piece of the pie" / "a slice of the pie"
When something valuable — like money, profits, power, or opportunity — is being divided among people, each person's share is called a "piece of the pie." For example: "The company grew rapidly, and everyone wanted a bigger slice of the pie."

"Pie in the sky"
This means an idea, plan, or hope that sounds wonderful but is unrealistic and unlikely to ever happen. For example: "His plan to retire at 25 is just pie in the sky."

"Eat humble pie"
This means to be forced to admit you were wrong and apologize, often in an embarrassing or humiliating way. For example: "He confidently predicted the team would lose, but after they won, he had to eat humble pie."

"Easy as pie"
This phrase means something is very easy. The pie itself here just represents something pleasant and effortless. For example: "Learning to ride a bike seemed hard at first, but it was easy as pie."

Pie chart: A circular diagram divided into wedge-shaped slices, where each slice represents a proportion or percentage of a whole. It is shaped like a pie viewed from above, with each "slice" showing how much of the total something represents.

Pie hole (informal/slang): A humorous or blunt way to refer to a person's mouth. "Shut your pie hole" is an informal way of telling someone to stop talking.

It helps to know where "pie" ends and other things begin:

  • Tart: A tart looks similar to a pie but typically has no top crust, a firmer and crispier pastry base, and is usually smaller and shallower. A tart is more refined and open; a pie is more enclosed and hearty. The line between the two can blur, but a tart is generally not called a pie.
  • Cobbler: A cobbler has a fruit filling at the bottom, but instead of a pastry crust on top, it has a layer of biscuit dough or cake batter. It's rustic and baked loose — not the neat, structured crust of a pie.
  • Pastry / Turnover: A small, folded individual-portion item (like an empanada or a hand pie) is related to a pie but often called a "hand pie" or "turnover" rather than a full pie.

A pie is a baked dish with a pastry crust and a filling — sweet or savory. The crust can wrap around the filling fully, partially, or just sit on top. Beyond food, "pie" is widely used in expressions to talk about sharing resources, unrealistic hopes, or admitting fault — and in the term "pie chart" for data visualization.

If you understand all of the above, you have a complete, lifetime grip on what the word "pie" means.
